title: Do Not Promote the Japanese Original-Vow Teaching
author: Long Ang

inline.s: [Editor's note] Master Hōnen and his followers loudly proclaimed: merely reciting the name ensures rebirth — no need to cultivate, no need to observe the precepts, no need to do good, no need to purify one's own mind, even committing evil all one's life is of no consequence.
The question is:
is it really true that merely reciting the name ensures rebirth?
Does this accord with the actual facts throughout the ages? If reciting the name truly ensured rebirth, why would our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha take the trouble to speak in
The Sūtra of Praise of the Pure Land, Embraced by the Buddhas

about the unbroken mindfulness of a single thought, and urge those who recite the Buddha's name to practice accordingly, free from doubt and from heedlessness? And how could the Buddhas of the ten directions (including Amitābha Buddha) praise and embrace this Dharma-door of unbroken mindfulness? If reciting the name truly ensured rebirth, why would Master Shandao — the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha — still need to speak of "right mindfulness at the deathbed" (see
Annotation on the "Text of Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at the Deathbed" of Master Shandao
article
) and "rebirth through continuity"
see
Master Shandao: Rebirth through Continuity
article
And why would Master Yongming — also Amitābha Buddha reborn — still need to speak of "the ten thoughts accomplished at death"?
(see
The Eighteenth Vow
article.) Therefore,
it is not the case that reciting the name alone ensures rebirth
(see
Does Reciting the Name Ensure Rebirth?

article.) If you believe their perverse doctrine and so are unable to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, yet fail to observe the precepts, fail to do good, and fail to purify your own mind — even committing evil all your life — then what awaits you
will surely be
the three evil paths, even the Avīci hell! (see
The Original-Vow Teaching Is a Non-Buddhist Cult Wrapped in Buddhism
Have you ever thought of this?
A single errant thought, and you suffer for kalpas upon kalpas — who can take your place?
Think on it! Think on it!

[Purifying one's own mind] This comes from the gāthā of the universal admonition of the seven Buddhas: "Commit no evil, practice all good, purify your own mind — this is the teaching of all Buddhas." It is the common admonition that the seven Buddhas of the past gave to the Buddha's disciples, and it is the general outline of Buddhist practice. The perverse doctrine proclaims "no need to observe the precepts" — that is to deny "commit no evil"; "no need to cultivate merit" — that is to deny "practice all good"; and furthermore there is no need to "purify one's own mind." Can this still be called Buddhism? [The seven Buddhas] refers to the seven Buddhas of the past: Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha.

[The ten thoughts accomplished at death] Master Yongming said: "If you wish the ten thoughts to be accomplished at death, simply prepare the means beforehand, gather your merit together, and dedicate it to that very moment; as long as thought after thought does not fail, you need have no worry." (From the Collected Works of Myriad Good Deeds Returning Together.) [Preparing the means beforehand] The term "means" (jinliang) means the ferry-crossing and the bridge; "to prepare the means beforehand" is to make everything ready in advance.

In recent years a countercurrent that must not be underestimated has been striking the Buddhist world of China with increasing severity. A small group of people argue that Chinese Buddhism should follow the path of Japanese Buddhism — that it should abandon the fine tradition of "monastic robes, vegetarian food, and celibacy" of Chinese Buddhism, and that the precepts should be relaxed. Worse still, some people,
with the support of vast foreign funds,

have illegally printed and distributed in great numbers the books of the Japanese Original-Vow teaching, doing their utmost to spread it. Some monks whose resolve for the Way is not firm — who find keeping the precepts and practicing too painful, or practicing in accord with the teaching too difficult — and some Buddhist cultivators of the Pure Land school who are unwilling to
faithfully

recite the Buddha's name wholeheartedly, eager for something easy, have been repeatedly cheated and deceived, and have muddle-headedly become believers and propagators of the Japanese Original-Vow teaching.
Let us look at some of the true circumstances of Japanese Buddhism and its Original-Vow teaching.

blocks.text: 1. Japanese Buddhism Has Fallen into the Predicament of Degeneration

inline.s: Chinese Buddhism is the center of northern Buddhism; the principal Mahāyāna scriptures of the Tripitaka and the Twelve Divisions have been preserved relatively completely through their Chinese translations. Over two thousand years, through the common dedication of the eminent monks and great masters of the Chinese Buddhist world, northern Mahāyāna Buddhism has not only flourished greatly in China but has gradually spread to Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Southeast Asia, and the countries of Europe and America.

Japan attaches great importance to Chinese Buddhism. For more than a thousand years it has not only sent great numbers of monks to study in China, but has also brought back most of the Chinese Buddhist scriptures. The Japanese have been quite diligent in the study of Buddhist doctrine and have achieved admirable results. The Chinese schools — the Huayan (Avatamsaka), the Tiantai, the Consciousness-only (Weishi), the Shingon (East-mandala Esoteric), and the Pure Land school — all have transmission in Japan, and there are still many Buddhists who practice in accord with the teaching. After Chinese Buddhism was transmitted there, the majority of the Japanese people came to believe in Buddhism.
In the course of its propagation, some Japanese Buddhist schools committed two serious errors:

The first error was to speak only of doctrinal study and not of observing the precepts and practicing. Japanese Buddhism is divided into two gateways: "the gateway of study" and "the gateway of practice." Many intellectuals take the path of study, treating Buddhism merely as a subject of scholarly research and sharply separating doctrine from practice. This group of Buddhists has various organizations — such as the well-known Sōka Gakkai — and they eagerly engage in politics; the Buddhist party of Japan has even become one of Japan's larger political parties, which is utterly at variance with the fine Chinese Buddhist tradition of non-involvement in politics. Those who follow the "gateway of practice" do not emphasize doctrinal study, nor do they teach the observance of precepts and cultivation; they engage only in drawing lots and fortune-telling and in conducting services for the dead.

The second error was that, eager for the convenient and the simple, they wrongly severed the scriptures and distorted the words of the Buddha and the patriarchs. For example, the Nichiren school requires only the recitation of "Namo Myōhō Renge Kyō" and a single phrase of "Namo Amitābha Buddha." They all abandon the precepts, allow monks to marry and raise children, and do not require the practice of good deeds or the bodhisattva path. The Jōdo Shinshū school of Japan requires only that one casually recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" with a heart of gratitude.

The consequence of these two erroneous views is that Japanese Buddhism has gradually come to have no monastic order of real precept-observing practitioners, but instead a great many "professional priests" who marry and raise children, drink wine and eat meat, and go to the temple to work by day. These professional priests go to the temples by day to tell fortunes, divine, and conduct services for the dead, and the money they earn belongs to them personally. There are quite a number of small temples in Japan, from a few dozen to two or three hundred square meters, each with a single priest, and the temple property and income all belong to that priest's family. Thus Japanese Buddhism, whose tradition valued "faith, understanding, practice, and realization" and which set store by precept-observance and cultivation, is now very far from Chinese Buddhism. Chinese Buddhism must never walk the road of Japanese Buddhism; otherwise it will surely decline rapidly.

Because the precepts are not taught and there are few true monastic communities and few true practitioners, Japanese Buddhism has degenerated and become in fact a cultural phenomenon. The Original-Vow teaching practiced by the Jōdo Shinshū school played a considerable role in the process of Japanese Buddhism's degeneration.

blocks.text: 2. The Japanese Original-Vow Teaching Was Established by Distorting the Scriptures

inline.s: The Japanese Original-Vow teaching is a school created by the Japanese monks Genshin (942–1017) and Hōnen (1133–1212). They distorted the scriptures and the original intentions of the patriarchs and, in order to establish their own school, set aside the basic doctrines of Buddhism and gave free rein to their own ideas, thereby acquiring considerable power to mislead. According to Hōnen's Selection of the Original Vow and Nianfo (Senchaku Hongan Nembutsushū) and the Essentials of the Pure School (Jingzong Yaozhi) of Oguri Ken'ichi, the basic tenets of the Original-Vow teaching may be summarized as follows:
1. The scriptures on which the Original-Vow teaching relies are the Three Pure Land Sūtras,

but it sets aside the "expedient means" of the Sūtra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the Amitābha Sūtra, selecting only the "true and real" Longer Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra (the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life); and within that sūtra it sets aside the forty-seven vows such as the Nineteenth and Twentieth Vows,
selecting only the Eighteenth Vow. One
complete
sūtra — apart from the Eighteenth Vow of the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life — is entirely
all
set aside, and it openly declares that the Holy Path is to be abandoned
(Note: The Amitābha Sūtra is the "sūtra guarded by the mindfulness of all Buddhas (including, of course, Amitābha Buddha)" praised by all the Buddhas. In the Amitābha Sūtra, Śākyamuni Buddha says:
In the Western world
there is a Buddha of Immeasurable Life,

and a Buddha of Immeasurable Marks, a Buddha of Immeasurable Banners, a Buddha of Great Light, a Buddha of Great Illumination, a Buddha of Jeweled Marks, a Buddha of Pure Radiance, and Buddhas like these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land stretching forth his long, broad tongue to cover the three-thousand great-thousand worlds and speaking truthful words: "You sentient beings,
should believe in this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit
and is guarded by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
This
sūtra, guarded by the mindfulness of all Buddhas,

has actually been slandered by them as a "false expedient" and so abolished. To slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma to such a degree! Can such people be reborn in the Western Pure Land? The roaring flames of hell are waiting for them!)

2. It distorts the Eighteenth Vow — "When I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions who hear my name, believe with utmost joy, and turn all their roots of good, thought after thought, toward being reborn in my land — even with ten thoughts, if they are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment; excepting only those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the true Dharma." It selects only the two phrases "hear my name, believe with utmost joy," and sets aside the rest, "all roots of good, thought after thought turned toward rebirth in my land," and so on. It says: as long as one has read the books propagating the Original-Vow teaching and heard its doctrine, then once one "gains faith," at that very moment one has attained the status
of determined rebirth
— regardless of when, where,
what
circumstance one dies in — even a Japanese soldier who cruelly killed Chinese people during the invasion of China and was killed in the fighting "is determinedly
reborn

in the Pure Land." It even says that as long as one has faith in the doctrine of the Original-Vow teaching, one is already reborn at that very instant, "dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression." Casual recitation of the Buddha-name is merely repaying the Buddha's kindness; even if one commits murder and arson, "entrusting oneself to the Buddha's power of salvation," one not only escapes punishment but is certain to be reborn in the Pure Land. They would even set aside the charge in the Eighteenth Vow of "excepting the five grave
offenses
, the slander of the true Dharma." They explicitly oppose giving, observing the precepts, practicing all good dharmas, and planting the roots of virtue; and they want no
repentance of
karmic hindrances, nor rejoicing in merit.
3. It advocates the doctrine of "pure other-power," holding that as long as one believes in the Original-Vow teaching and trusts that the power of the Buddha's original vow is inconceivable,
one need not exert the slightest self-power and need not
observe the precepts
or cultivate; "entrusting oneself to the Buddha's salvation" is enough. It requires one to "set aside the former giving, precept-observance,
and even the various practices such as honoring one's parents,"

saying that all these various practices are sundry cultivation. As long as one believes in the Original-Vow teaching, one immediately obtains the "certificate of the status of rebirth"; everything is handed over to the Buddha's arrangement, and lying on the great ship of Amitābha's original vow, naturally and comfortably, one arrives in the Pure Land as soon as one wakes from sleep. They guarantee it with a warranty: "If one is a follower of our school, one will certainly be reborn and will become a Buddha."
4. It opposes causality and
proclaims
"what he does, I receive," rejecting "what I do, I reap." Originally,
of rebirth in the Pure Land
the proper cause
is the practitioner's own perfect endowment of the three provisions of faith, vow, and recitation of the name; the Buddha's power is only the augmenting condition (adhipati) of rebirth.
But
the Original-Vow teaching
instead

nonsensically asserts that the matter of rebirth is such that "the Buddha has already accomplished it for me; he gives this accomplishment to you for nothing — will you not take it?" Among the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice, it mentions only faith in the Buddha's power — that is, faith in pure other-power — while opposing faith in self, faith in cause, faith in effect, faith in things, and faith in principle.

5. It opposes arousing the bodhi-mind and practicing the bodhisattva path. Arousing the supreme bodhi-mind and practicing the bodhisattva path are the cause of Buddhahood, yet the Original-Vow teaching gives the nonsense that "although the three higher grades raise other practices such as the bodhi-mind, Śākyamuni did not praise other practices." It openly slanders Śākyamuni as "not praising" the bodhi-mind and the other practices such as the bodhisattva path — truly audacious

Anyone with even a slight knowledge of basic Buddhist studies can see at a glance that the above fallacies of the Japanese Original-Vow teaching are contrary to the Buddhist scriptures, extremely wrong, and a very harmful wrong path. It has already brought an irrecoverable calamity upon Japanese Buddhism. We must resolutely, and on solid grounds, refute it point by point.

blocks.text: 3. The Patriarchs and Great Masters of Our Land Severely Denounced the Japanese Original-Vow Teaching

inline.s: The patriarchs and great masters of our land, through the generations, all walked the path of arousing the bodhi-mind, strictly observing the precepts, widely practicing the six perfections, persistently nurturing merit and wisdom, and being perfectly endowed with faith, vow, and practice, thereby being reborn in the Western Pure Land; they all consistently
held the
view that the Pure Land teaching is the Dharma-door of twofold power and firmly opposed "pure other-power." Therefore
not a single patriarch or great master has propagated the Original-Vow teaching
and indeed quite a number of patriarchs and great masters have severely denounced its true nature.

At the beginning of this century, the great lay master Yang Renshan of the Chinese Buddhist world criticized item by item the Essentials of the Pure School (Jingzong Yaozhi) and the Selection of the Original Vow and Nianfo (Senchaku Hongan Nembutsushū). Master Renshan said that "one who is silent in upholding the true Dharma prizes it above his own life," and so he fiercely attacked the Original-Vow teaching. As the Original-Vow teaching declared that the Holy Path was to be abandoned, Renshan said: "The World-Honored One Amitābha accomplished the original vow through the Holy Path. If one says
"abandon"
the Holy Path, then one goes against the original vow. Since cause and effect are opposed, how could one attain rebirth

"Those who are reborn in the Western land also realize the excellent fruit through the Holy Path." "Faith arises from one's own mind; other-power is the other-power that one's own mind sees." "Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas ... the bodhi-mind is the mind wherein cause and effect interpenetrate each other ... if one abandons the bodhi-mind, one does not know by means of what one becomes a Buddha
"Now to emphasize the recitation of the Buddha-name while slighting the bodhi-mind greatly violates the teaching
"Fabricating a Dharma out of an ordinary person's speculation and setting it above the scriptures — the guilt reaches to heaven
"To interpret the text according to its literal meaning brings the resentment of the Buddhas of the three times
but to deviate a single word from the sūtra is to speak the words of a demon."

The contemporary great masters Master Yinshun and Master Sheng-yen have long been critical of the degeneration of Japanese Buddhism and of Jōdo Shinshū. The world-recognized contemporary Pure Land master Master Jingkong also recently gave an explicit instruction: "To merely teach the ten thoughts at the hour of death, and say that even a single thought ensures rebirth, while in ordinary life one need not observe the precepts and may act recklessly and commit karmic offenses ... at the time of death, do you have the assurance of
rebirth
?" "To promote the original vow while abandoning precept-observance is to walk a dangerous path
indeed

! ... They have completely misunderstood the Buddha's meaning and distorted it." He denounced it severely: "To promote the Original-Vow recitation of the Buddha-name — that kills people!" "Now there are some who promote the Original-Vow recitation of the Buddha-name:
make the vow to seek rebirth and you are determinately reborn
Is it really that simple? Only when the vow contains practice is this vow a true vow
"How can one say that making a vow without practice can lead to rebirth? The Buddha never said such a thing."
Some say that Master Yinguang and the lay master Huang Nianzu have spoken of the importance of the original-vow other-power
But they never promoted the Original-Vow teaching

on the contrary, they repeatedly emphasized the importance of the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice. The book of the lay master Huang Nianzu is even entitled Pure Land Provisions (Jingtu Ziliang). It may be said that from ancient times down to the present, no patriarch or great master of China has
ever
promoted the Original-Vow teaching. The Japanese Original-Vow teaching calls the Chinese masters Tanluan

Daochuo, and Shandao the three patriarchs of the Original-Vow teaching; and though they all stressed that the power of Amitābha's original vow is inconceivable, their writings and their practice alike prove that they were great beings who aroused the bodhi-mind, broadly delivered sentient beings, strictly upheld the prohibitive precepts, and practiced with vigor — and they all emphasized that Amitābha's original vow is the augmenting condition (adhipati) of rebirth. Master Shandao also earnestly taught that "matters of birth and death are of great importance; one must exert one's own effort to attain them,"
and he advocated the doctrine of "self-power and other-power together" and opposed the doctrine of "pure other-power."

Recently the well-known great master, the lay master Zheng Songying, has cried out with eager urgency to "destroy the wrong and reveal the right." He fiercely denounced the Japanese Original-Vow teaching as "evil and demonic," and emphasized that the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice must all be fully present before "the ten thousand cultivators all go." He asked in reproach: "The Original-Vow teaching requires only a single act of faith, completely without practice, relying wholly on other-power and wanting no self-power — is this still Buddhism?" With compassion and earnestness he sounded the warning bell for us: "Towards such perverse doctrines, which wholly contradict the teaching, mislead sentient beings, and are extremely harmful, we
must
deeply criticize them and resolutely reject them. I respectfully beg the four assemblies and my teachers and friends to
destroy the wrong and reveal the right.

blocks.text: 4. The Original-Vow Teaching Was a Tool of Japanese Militarism's Invasion of China

inline.s: In the Second World War, Japanese militarism launched the war of aggression against China and committed monstrous crimes — above all the bloody slaughter of the Chinese people, wantonly killing all, looting all, and burning all, inflicting on the Chinese people suffering of immeasurable depth. To this day, many Japanese still refuse to admit their error in this war, refusing that it was "aggression" and a "crime," insisting instead that it was a "holy
war."

Why are these Japanese so unable to distinguish good from evil? Apart from other causes, it is related to the fact that the main sects of Japanese Buddhism, commonly believed in by the Japanese people, have lost the function of urging people to do good. Japanese Buddhism, abandoning precept-observance and cultivation and encouraging the taking of life, has discarded the basic Buddhist principle of "commit no evil, practice all good"; and by openly proclaiming that "the five grave offenses and slandering the Dharma are of no account, and that merely believing the original vow ensures"
rebirth,"
it is in effect proclaiming that killing is without guilt, that robbery is without guilt, that rape is without guilt, and that slandering the true Dharma is without guilt. These views
exactly suit
the taste of the Japanese militarists, and the Original-Vow teaching has degenerated into the spiritual pillar and shameful tool of the Japanese militarist aggressors.
During the period of
the Japanese invasion of China,

quite a number of priests of the Japanese Original-Vow teaching served with the army, and built Japanese Honganji temples in many places in China, such as Nanjing and Wuhu in Anhui. The Japanese priests encouraged the Japanese soldiers, telling them that even those who had killed Chinese people could enter the Pure Land, and they made a specialty of conducting services for fallen Japanese soldiers, thereby becoming accomplices in the Japanese invasion of China. The Chinese people, who had suffered bitterly from Japanese aggression, long ago came to hate the Japanese Original-Vow teaching deeply

and with Japan's surrender these priests of the Japanese Honganji temples could only flee China with their tails between their legs. During the period of Japanese rule, many Honganji temples were also built in various parts of China's Taiwan Province. After the recovery of Taiwan, these priests of the Japanese Original-Vow teaching also shamefully rolled out of Taiwan. The facts prove that the Chinese people have long loathed the Japanese Original-Vow teaching and have long seen clearly its reactionary nature.

blocks.text: 5. Resolutely Smash the Onslaught of the Japanese Original-Vow Teaching

inline.s: The Japanese people and the Chinese people are friendly neighbors separated only by a strip of water. The truly right-believing Buddhists of Japan and the right-believing Buddhists of China are all disciples of the Buddha, fellow cultivators and companions in study, bound by a thousand years of friendship. But there are in Japan certain militarists whose heart to bully China and destroy our Chinese nation has not died. After their military aggression failed, they engaged in economic aggression, and when economic aggression had little effect, they plotted cultural aggression to bring down China. In recent years they have plotted to use the Japanese Original-Vow teaching as a breakthrough in cultural faith in order to gradually take control of China. In the 1990s the Japanese Original-Vow teaching was re-transmitted to China's Taiwan
and then gradually to mainland China.
They are willing to spend tens of millions of funds to spread the Japanese Original-Vow teaching; the background of this deserves deep reflection

There are a few, though, who vigorously spread the Original-Vow teaching and attack China's traditional Buddhism, becoming their tools. We must shout loudly at these people: we hope you will quickly rein in your horse at the cliff and turn back to the shore.

The spread of the Original-Vow teaching in China has tended to spread rapidly; this is mainly because it has a market among two groups of people. A small number of younger monastics, who have not established a true resolve for the Way and know very little about Buddhist doctrine — some of whom have taken ordination precisely in order to "find employment" in Buddhism — are best catered to by the promise that they may drink wine, eat meat, and gamble, may marry and raise children, and need not observe the precepts; such priests are truly comfortable and all too easy to be, so they naturally welcome it. The other group consists of some lay Buddhists who do not understand the doctrine. They believe in the Pure Land teaching and earnestly hope to be reborn in the Western Pure Land at the end of their lives, yet they feel no confidence in their own rebirth. As soon as they hear that the Original-Vow teaching can give a warranty and guarantee their rebirth, being eager for something easy, they are easily deceived and pulled over to the Original-Vow teaching. There are also some who have read many Buddhist books without understanding them, who are likewise willing to observe the precepts and cultivate, but are deceived by the Original-Vow teaching's fraud of claiming to come from the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life and to have been advocated by Master Shandao. After being captured they even join the ranks of cross-regional propagation of the Original-Vow teaching and do foolish things that harm China's Buddhist cause. The deception of these Buddhists by the Japanese Original-Vow teaching is temporary; once they earnestly learn the fact that the Original-Vow teaching once served as a tool of the Japanese aggression against China and is a distorted teaching that twists the scriptures and the patriarchs' intent, they will surely soon return to the correct path. You are Buddhists of Chinese Buddhism, not adherents of Japanese Buddhism, and you are certain to come back. We ardently hope that you will leave the Original-Vow teaching and return to the authentic Chinese Pure Land teaching.

The cult organization Falun Gong requires its followers only to practice its cultivation behind closed doors and not to concern themselves with the affairs of others, forbidding its disciples to donate money or give loving-kindness in flood relief, valuing only "protecting the teaching" and not teaching the doing of good. The Original-Vow teaching requires that doing good and performing virtuous deeds all be abandoned, and denounces them as "sundry practices." Li Hongzhi says that as long as one believes in Falun Gong, he can carry one into heaven; the Original-Vow teaching says that as long as one believes in the Original-Vow teaching, they guarantee you will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land and immediately become a Buddha. Li Hongzhi says that if he installs a "Dharma Wheel" in your belly, you need not practice qigong and all your illnesses will vanish, and his "Dharma body" will ensure your safety in all things; the Original-Vow teaching says that as long as you believe in the Original-Vow teaching, without doing good or accumulating merit you can be reborn and become a Buddha — and even if you commit evil all your life it is of no account, for you may "entrust yourself to Amitābha's salvation." The Original-Vow teaching deifies the Buddha, making the Buddha like the savior "God." They arbitrarily pick and choose among the words of the Buddha and the sayings of the patriarchs, willfully distort Buddhist doctrine, and maliciously oppose the precepts laid down by the Buddha — truly betraying the teacher and destroying the ancestors, audacious

They themselves can never be reborn in the Pure Land, but will only fall into hell — how truly pitiful. The conduct of the Original-Vow teaching and that of the cult organization Falun Gong are so alike
This indeed deserves our high vigilance.
The Japanese Original-Vow teaching has
spent huge sums of money

printing illegal publications and proselytizing in China on a large scale, vainly hoping to establish a new sect and to invade the spiritual faith of the Chinese people through cultural means. If it is allowed to develop freely until, as in Japan, it establishes a powerful reactionary party like the "Buddhist Party," it will have an incalculable destructive effect on the good situation of China's stability and unity.
We must also not underestimate the impact and destructive effect of the spread of the Original-Vow teaching on Chinese Buddhism; we must in no way treat it lightly and let it develop freely.

If a considerable number of young monks come to believe in the Original-Vow teaching and abandon the observance of precepts, then Chinese Buddhism will no longer be true Buddhism, the Buddha's true Dharma will vanish several thousand years before its time, people's Dharma-body wisdom-life will be destroyed, and the Buddha's Dharma-life will be at an end — what a dreadful prospect this is

Must we not wake up with a start and rise to wage a resolute struggle against the Japanese Original-Vow teaching? We must not take "going along with circumstances" as an excuse, nor say that because we have not resolved to practice exclusively the Pure Land teaching we will just let the Original-Vow teaching take its
own

course; rather, we should sincerely learn from the eminent monks and great masters who are courageous in destroying the wrong and revealing the right, raise high the banner of Dharma, criticize the Japanese Original-Vow teaching with a clear-cut stand, and beat back this countercurrent
